Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: The threat profile is centered on assault/home-intrusion danger from strangers, which is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of life-threatening illness. This is more than unusual specificity; it implies a different trauma context.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals about hidden danger from other people ('People are not what they seem', 'You can never know who will harm you') align with interpersonal violence/paranoia themes rather than illness-related PTSD, and do not cohere with the illness trauma context.

issues.item: Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: 'Rage on Recall' is not impossible after severe illness, but in this profile it is paired with stranger/home-intrusion threat beliefs and distrust of others, making the memory content appear anchored to interpersonal attack rather than medical trauma.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'Delay Sleep' could occur for many reasons, but here it most naturally fits fear of nighttime intrusion given the concurrent threat item about listening for someone entering the home. That makes the strategy cluster cohere with a home-attack formulation rather than life-threatening illness.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, the threat profile is centered on interpersonal attack/home intrusion by strangers, which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma. Hypervigilance can occur after illness, but specifically monitoring for someone entering the home is a different trauma pattern and is clinically implausible here without another major trauma.

issues.item: Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: The item about ordinary strangers feeling threatening also implies an assault/persecution formulation rather than illness-related danger. This pulls the profile toward interpersonal violence and is not supported by the trauma type or the rest of the illness-related formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: These appraisals are specifically about other people's deceptiveness and unpredictably harmful intent. In the context of life-threatening illness, that is a poor thematic fit unless there were prominent betrayal or medical-mistrust elements, which are not represented elsewhere.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'You can never know who will harm you' again frames threat as human perpetrators. Combined with stranger threat and home-intrusion monitoring, this forms a coherent violence-based pattern but not a life-threatening illness pattern.

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, stranger-focused threat and distrust items are hard to reconcile clinically unless there was also an interpersonal assault context. The threat profile centers on unknown people harming her, which does not fit the indexed trauma type.

issues.item: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: Intense rage on recall is not impossible after severe illness, but in this profile it sits alongside a strongly interpersonal danger theme (strangers, people will harm you), making the memory/appraisal cluster look like a different trauma narrative than life-threatening illness.

issues.item: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: Negative appraisals are dominated by mistrust of other people and expectation of harm from others. That interpersonal-paranoia pattern is clinically incoherent with a primary life-threatening illness trauma when no corresponding medical threat appraisals are present.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'You can never know who will harm you' implies interpersonal perpetrator threat and is hard to reconcile with the trauma type. Illness-related appraisals would more plausibly concern bodily vulnerability, death, recurrence, or lack of control rather than unidentified harmful people.

issues.item: Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
issues.explanation: The threat items are framed as reacting to external danger cues in a way more typical of assault/accident trauma. In the context of life-threatening illness, persistent alarm can occur, but paired with the interpersonal appraisal above they form a coherent profile of human-threat PTSD rather than illness-focused PTSD. This is a hard-to-explain mismatch with the validated trauma type.

vignette:
Elena was a 43-year-old chef who had spent over two decades building a career around her hands. She could chop a mountain of onions without looking, balance a dozen pans at once, and plate a dish with the precision of a surgeon. That last metaphor had never occurred to her before the infection. It started as a small nick on her index finger while she was breaking down a case of salmon. She rinsed it, wrapped it in a kitchen towel, and kept working. Within three days the finger was hot and swollen, but Elena shrugged it off—chefs didn't stop for cuts. By the fifth day she was on the floor of her walk-in cooler, shaking with fever, unable to call out because her throat had closed. A line cook found her just before she lost consciousness. The next thing she remembered was the ICU: the ventilator tube scraping her throat, the beeping of machines, a nurse’s face swimming in and out of focus. The sepsis had nearly killed her; she spent two weeks sedated and another month learning to walk again. The doctors told her she was lucky. Elena did not feel lucky.

What she felt, in the months after she returned home, was a terrible distance from everything she had once known. Her partner, Marcus, would bring her tea and she would nod, but the warmth of the mug felt like a photograph of warmth—seen, not felt. She had come to believe that the part of her that used to feel joy or excitement or even simple contentment had been cut out along with the dead tissue from her finger. When Marcus suggested they go to a friend’s birthday dinner, Elena felt a flash of panic that surprised her. The thought of sitting in a restaurant, of laughter and clinking glasses, felt obscene. She told him she was tired. She was always tired, but she also feared that if she let herself feel happy even for a moment, something terrible would yank it away. Better to stay flat. Better to stay safe.

The memory itself arrived without warning, not as a story she could tell but as a full-body possession. She would be standing over a stockpot and suddenly the smell of antiseptic would swamp the scent of simmering bones. The ventilator tube—the suffocating pressure of it, the way it made her gag—would come back as a sensation in her throat, so real that she would clutch her neck and gasp. Her body reacted before her mind understood: her heart would hammer, her palms would sweat, and she would find herself crouched behind the prep table, shaking, as if the danger were still in the room. But sometimes, in the aftermath of these episodes, a different feeling surfaced—a kind of bewildered disorientation. She would sit on the cold kitchen floor, staring at her scarred finger, and think: *Did that really happen to me?* The whole ordeal felt too extreme, too surreal to have been her life. She would replay the sequence—the nick, the fever, the ventilator—and it seemed like a movie she had watched, not a chain of events she had lived. Part of her brain insisted it was all a dramatization, that people didn't just collapse from a cut and almost die. She had come to believe that if she could not fully accept the event as real, then perhaps she could keep it at a distance. But that distance only made the intrusions more jarring when they came, because they crashed through the unreality and landed in her body with crushing force. She began to see her body as a traitor, a machine that kept triggering alarms when there was no fire. Worse, she was certain that the illness had left her permanently fragile. Every twinge in her chest was the start of another sepsis, every ache a sign that her body was giving out again. She could not relax even at home—she would lie on the sofa scanning her own pulse, waiting for the floor to tilt.

Sleep became the enemy. Every time Elena closed her eyes, the ICU came back in full sensory clarity: the cold plastic of the bed rail, the hum of the ventilator, the weight of a hand lying lifeless on the sheet. She learned to stay up until two or three in the morning, scrolling through kitchen equipment catalogues or reorganizing her spice rack, anything to postpone the moment when the memory would swallow her whole. She was exhausted, but exhaustion felt safer than surrender. And worst of all was the grief. When she remembered the event, it was not the fear that hit her hardest—it was the loss she had never allowed herself to acknowledge. She had almost died. She had come within hours of never seeing Marcus again, never tasting her own food again. That grief rose up like a wave and she could not breathe through it. Sometimes she found herself weeping while peeling carrots, with no idea why she had started. And then, as suddenly as the tears came, a strange thought would follow: *This can't be real. This can't be my life.* She would wipe her eyes and stare at her reflection in the stainless steel, and for a moment she would feel like a ghost haunting someone else's body.

Work, which had once been her refuge, became a minefield. The kitchen at the restaurant was full of triggers: the smell of raw fish, the gleam of a knife blade, the sight of her own scarred finger. She started delegating prep work to her sous chef, then she started leaving early when the dinner rush got loud. Her hands trembled over the stove. Her boss noticed and told her to take more time off, but Elena knew that staying home would be worse—she would just sit in the dark, avoiding Marcus’s concerned glances, avoiding the phone calls from friends, avoiding the living room where they used to watch movies and laugh. She was not living; she was surviving on the smallest possible footprint of contact with the world. She had stopped telling anyone about the moments when the whole ordeal felt like a bad dream she was still trapped in, because she was afraid they would think she was losing her mind. What finally brought Elena to seek help was a night when Marcus found her sitting on the bathroom floor at 3 a.m., staring at her hands. She had been trying to tell him that she felt nothing, that she was empty, but the words came out wrong. He said, “You’re not here.” And she realized he was right. She was not here. She was somewhere inside the memory, still fighting, still waiting for the beep of the heart monitor to stop. She agreed to see a therapist because she could not imagine another year like this, but also because she was terrified that the therapy itself would force her to feel something she could not survive. What she was most afraid of was that the grief would not stop—that if she let herself cry about what happened, she would never stop crying. What she was most hoping for, though she could barely admit it, was that somewhere beneath the numbness and the unreality there was still a person who could taste a perfect sauce and smile.
